title: Task 1 ground rules
blocks: Word limit — how many words to write
The rule is a minimum of 150 words. But no upper limit is given, so everyone asks: what is the maximum? The answer in one word — 180.
Never fewer than 150. Even if you write 148 words, you lose marks.
Don't go above 200. The more words, the more chances of mistakes, and the less time for Task 2 (which carries double the weight).
The space on the answer sheet easily fits an answer of 170–180 words. If you need an extra sheet, you'll know you are writing too much.
What counts as a word and what doesn't
IELTS's official rule is simple: everything you write is a word — a, an, the, in, of, numbers (2010), percentages — everything. A hyphenated word is one word (twenty-five = 1 word).
But keep two things in mind:

Sentences copied word for word from the question are not "your writing" in the examiner's eyes. Even if those words are counted, they are not taken as evidence of your ability; on the contrary, they give the impression that you "can't paraphrase".

Examiners don't sit and count words — they don't have that much time. They estimate the length by eye. So don't waste time counting in the exam hall; instead, find out beforehand how many lines 170 words take up in your handwriting (usually 12–14 lines).
Any piece of writing has three parts: introduction, body, conclusion. In Task 1 we will write four paragraphs:
What the visual shows — in your own words
The 2–3 biggest features, without any numbers
Details of the first group, with numbers
Details of the second group, with numbers and comparisons

**Why is the overview the second paragraph?** Many books tell you to write the overview at the end as a "conclusion". That works too, but there is a risk: if you run out of time, the overview is what gets left out, and without an overview a whole band is lost in Task Achievement. So write the overview right after the introduction. If you have time, you can add a one-line closing sentence at the end — no harm if you don't.
The body can also have three paragraphs if the data naturally falls into three parts; but two is the safe default.

The IELTS authority says 20 minutes for Task 1. The reason: in Task 1 all the data is given, so once you learn the method, writing it is comparatively easy. Task 2 carries much more importance and weight.
Read the visual, understand the axis/unit/legend, mark the main points

We say it firmly: never take more than 20 minutes on Task 1 under any circumstances. Many people write Task 1 very carefully and at length, then rush to finish Task 2 — that's a bad bargain. When 20 minutes are up, finish the sentence you are on and move to Task 2.
In IELTS, roughly 7 types of Task 1 appear:

Most of the time a single type appears on its own. Sometimes a combination of two types appears (e.g. bar chart + pie chart). How to write each type is shown in detail with graphs in the following parts; so for now just remember the names.

Task 1 assesses whether you can describe the given data well. So any opinion, any explanation of "why this happened", any advice — is completely forbidden. "I think / I believe / probably because of the pandemic" — even one sentence like this lowers Task Achievement, because that information is not in the chart.
The report is impersonal. Write The chart shows…, never We can see… or You can notice….
3. Never start writing without fully understanding the graph (V.V.I)

Read everything — the title, the labels of both axes, the unit, the legend. Ask yourself: what is being measured? In which unit? Over what period? How many categories? Start writing only when you can explain it to yourself in one sentence. If you start writing before understanding it, you end up describing the wrong thing.
The first sentence (The graph shows…) is always in the present tense.
If the visual has past years, describe the data in the past tense: Sales rose in 2010.
If there is no year, use the present: Most households recycle glass.
If there are future years, not will/shall — write: is expected / projected / forecast / predicted / anticipated to + verb: Solar output is expected to triple by 2030.
Process and diagram → present simple, usually passive: The pulp is then dried.

No, it's optional. If an overview is written, the conclusion only repeats it. If you have time write one line; if not, leave it out — it won't affect your score. If you write one, it is a summary; never an opinion.

**Task 1 — what to avoid (avoid-list)**
▸ No opinion / advice / explanation of causes.
▸ No I, we, you.
▸ No copying sentences from the question.
▸ Never write without an overview; no numbers in the overview.
▸ No writing out every number one by one ("data dump").
▸ Not the same trend verb or the same connective three times.
▸ In a combination task, don't compare one graph with another — comparison is always within the same graph. (If there are several pie charts, compare between the pies.)
▸ Not more than 200 words, not more than 20 minutes.
▸ No bullets, headings or notes — paragraphs in full sentences.

**Task 1 — what to make sure of (must-list)**
**For line, column/bar and pie charts:**
▸ If there is a chance to compare, always compare.
▸ Always use connective words.
▸ Use synonyms for the question's words as far as possible (shows → illustrates; number → figure; percentage → proportion).
▸ If no time is mentioned, present tense; if it is, the tense that matches that time.
▸ If there are several pie charts, inter-compare between the pies.
**For flow charts and diagrams:**
▸ Passive form in most cases.
▸ Cycle or non-cycle — pay attention. If it is a cycle, you can start the description from any point you like; if not a cycle, from the starting point.
▸ If the diagram has specific segmentation (divisions), paragraph according to those divisions.
▸ Above all: describe by following the arrows.
▸ A conclusion isn't needed; if no time is mentioned, present tense (flow charts usually don't have one).
Language of numbers and comparison — needed in every type
Preposition — the most common grammar mistake in Task 1
Wrong preposition = wrong data = lower Task Achievement. "increased to 20%" and "increased by 20%" mean completely different things.
roughly, approximately, about, around, nearly, almost, just under, just over, a little more than, close to
half, a third, a quarter, three-quarters, one in five, one in ten, twice as many as, three times higher than, double, treble
higher / lower than, far more than, slightly less than, the same as, similar to, in contrast to, compared with, whereas, while, respectively
the highest, the lowest, the second largest, followed by, at the bottom, the only one to fall, the majority, the minority

title: Line Graph step by step: Introduction and Overview
blocks: The line graph comes up most often, and what you learn here (introduction, overview, the language of trends, comparison) is what you'll use in every other type. So read this part slowly and attentively.

You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
The graph below shows the number of visitors (in thousands) to Greenhill National Park between 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
You should write at least 150 words.
I'll teach two methods of writing the introduction: (1) the Five-Question Method, (2) the Sentence-Frame Method. Learn both; in the exam, use whichever comes to mind faster.
Find the answers to five questions from the graph — you'll get all the ingredients of the introduction:
1. What type of graph is it?
visitors more than doubled overall, with a big drop in the mid-2010s
Just arrange the first four answers together and you have the first sentence:
The line graph shows the number of visitors to a national park, in thousands, from 1990 to 2020.
But this is almost a copy of the question. Now let's change the words:
illustrates, depicts, gives information about, presents, compares (if there are several lines)
how many people visited, visitor numbers, the figures for visitors, the amount of visitors (✗ — people are countable, so number/how many)
"in + unit" structure: in thousands / in metric tonnes / in per cent / in US dollars
from 1990 to 2020 · over a thirty-year period ending in 2020 · over three decades from 1990 · for 30 years up to 2020 · in the period 1990–2020
Six structures for the duration — avoid the one in the question and take a different one:
For (period) up to ______ (For 30 years up to 2020)
From ______ for the next/following (period) (From 1990 for the next 30 years)
Over a period of ______ up to ______ (Over a period of 30 years up to 2020)
In ______ (when there is only a single year)
Now add answer number 5 as the second sentence. The full introduction:

The line graph illustrates how many people visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, over the thirty years from 1990 to 2020. Visitor numbers more than doubled over the period despite a sharp fall in the mid-2010s.
In this method you fill in the blanks of a fixed format with information from the question:

**Sentence 1:** The [line / bar / column graph · pie chart · table · diagram] + [describes / exhibits / illustrates / compares / demonstrates / indicates] + [information — paraphrased] + [measurement — in + unit] + [duration]
**Sentence 2:** Gist — highest / lowest / biggest rise / biggest fall — any one of them.
Three more kinds of introduction for the same graph — notice that the words and order are different in each, and the gist is different too:
The line graph describes the number of people who visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, between 1990 and 2020. The lowest figures were recorded in the first five years.
The given line graph demonstrates the annual visitor figures for Greenhill National Park, measured in thousands, from 1990 for the following three decades. Attendance peaked in 2020.
Visitor numbers at Greenhill National Park have been depicted through the line graph in thousands over a period of 30 years up to 2020. The steepest decline occurred between 2010 and 2015.
An introduction written in a slightly uncommon format helps you get a higher score. But be careful — the first sentence of the introduction must be in the present tense.
Overview = the 2–3 biggest points of the graph, without any numbers. What you can say:
When / which is highest and lowest
The position at the end compared with the start
Any major exception (a big slump, a crossover)
With several lines: who is at the top and who is at the bottom at the end
Words to start with: Overall, … / It is clear that … / The most striking feature is …
Overall, visitor numbers rose considerably over the period, although the growth was interrupted by a sharp decline in the mid-2010s. The figure at the end of the period was the highest recorded.

title: Line Graph: Body, trend language and Conclusion
blocks: In the body paragraphs we will describe the main information of the graph. How much you write will depend on how much information the graph has:
If the graph has a lot of information, write only the main / significant data and trends.
If the graph has little information, you have to describe almost all of it — because under 150 words means negative marking.
comparison of start and end; two equal values

As soon as you get the question, mark all the significant points and trends on the graph (you can mark the IELTS question paper as you like). Give a number to every trend you have marked — then you'll know how many things you need to discuss:
5 trends are marked in the picture

To explain each change you need a verb (direction: did it rise or fall). Changes differ in type / size, so the verb needs an adverb (how strongly / how much). You also need to say over what period and by how much it changed. In other words, a trend description has five things:

**Subject + verb + adverb + time + amount changed**
Visitor numbers + rose + sharply + between 1995 and 2005 + to 480,000.
remained stable / steady / constant / unchanged, stayed at, levelled off, plateaued, maintained the same level, showed no change
stability, a plateau, a levelling-off, no change
rose, increased, grew, climbed, went up, ascended
a rise, an increase, growth, a climb
soared, surged, jumped, rocketed, shot up, leapt, boomed
a surge, a jump, a boom, a leap
fell, declined, decreased, dropped, dipped, went down, reduced
a fall, a decline, a decrease, a drop, a dip
plunged, plummeted, slumped, collapsed, dived, halved
a plunge, a slump, a collapse
peaked at, reached a high / low of, hit a low of, bottomed out at
a peak, a high, a low, a trough
Adverbs / adjectives by size of change
dramatically, sharply, steeply, considerably, significantly, substantially, markedly, drastically, rapidly, quickly
dramatic, sharp, steep, considerable, significant, substantial, marked, drastic, rapid
slightly, marginally, a little, minimally, slowly
Trend 1 needs no adverb, because there is no change. For the rest, choose the right adverb, and for similar changes don't repeat the same adverb — take a different one.
Now sentences for each trend — in three formats
Each trend can be written in three ways: (a) verb + adverb, (b) There was a + adjective + noun, (c) a single strong verb (no adverb). In the exam, mix all three so that the structure doesn't repeat.
(a) The number of visitors remained constant / stable / unchanged at 200,000 between 1990 and 1995.
(b) There was no change in visitor numbers for the first five years, which stayed at 200,000.
(c) Visitor numbers plateaued at 200,000 from 1990 to 1995.
(a) Visitor numbers rose sharply / increased dramatically / grew rapidly by 280,000 to 480,000 between 1995 and 2005.
(b) There was a dramatic / sharp / steep rise of 280,000 in the following decade, to 480,000.
(c) Attendance soared / surged / jumped to 480,000 in 2005, more than double the 1995 figure.
(a) The figure then fell slightly / dipped marginally by 10,000 to 470,000 in 2010.
(b) There was a slight / marginal / small dip in numbers over the next five years, to 470,000.
(a) Visitors fell sharply / dropped steeply / declined considerably by 120,000 to 350,000 between 2010 and 2015.
(b) There was a sharp / steep / considerable fall of 120,000 in the next five years, to 350,000.
(c) Attendance plunged / slumped / plummeted to 350,000 in 2015.
(a) The number climbed strongly / rose markedly by 170,000 to a peak of 520,000 in the last five years.
(b) There was a strong / marked recovery in the final period, with numbers reaching a high of 520,000.
(c) Visitors rebounded / recovered to a record 520,000 in 2020.
Extra: fluctuation — not in this graph, but it comes up in the exam
(a) The figure fluctuated considerably / varied widely between 300,000 and 430,000 over the period.
(b) There was considerable fluctuation in the figure, which moved between 300,000 and 430,000.
(c) Numbers oscillated between roughly 300,000 and 430,000 throughout.
Six ways to change the sentence order
To bring variety to the structure with the same information, you can move the elements around:
Information + verb + adverb + time + amount: Visitor numbers fell sharply between 2010 and 2015 by 120,000.
Information + verb + adverb + amount + time: Visitor numbers fell sharply by 120,000 between 2010 and 2015.
Time + information + verb + adverb + amount: Between 2010 and 2015, visitor numbers fell sharply by 120,000.
There was a + adjective + noun + in + information + time: There was a sharp fall of 120,000 in visitor numbers between 2010 and 2015.
Information + saw / experienced / recorded + a + adjective + noun + time: Visitor numbers saw a sharp fall between 2010 and 2015.
Time + saw + a + adjective + noun + in + information: The period 2010–2015 saw a sharp fall in visitor numbers.
Remember that repetition of structure and vocabulary will lower your score. And use connective words wherever applicable.

Let's split the five trends into two paragraphs: the first paragraph trends 1–2, the second paragraph trends 3–5. For each trend we pick one of the three formats above — so that the structure doesn't repeat:

For the first five years the number of visitors remained constant at 200,000. After 1995, however, the figure grew rapidly, reaching 480,000 in 2005, more than double the starting level.

This was followed by a decade of decline. Numbers dipped slightly to 470,000 in 2010 and then fell sharply to 350,000 over the next five years. In the final period the trend reversed, and visitors climbed to a peak of 520,000 in 2020, the highest figure recorded.
Notice: every sentence has a number, direction, degree and time; no structure appears twice; the connectives (however, this was followed by, then, in the final period) guide the reader.

A Task 1 conclusion is basically a summary of the whole task. It is optional — leave it out if you don't have time. If you do, take a concluding connective from the connective list and write one sentence: a notable point, or an overall summary.
In summary / To sum up / To recapitulate, despite the setback after 2010, the park attracted far more visitors at the end of the period than at the beginning.
Always remember: **no personal opinion may be written in a Task 1 conclusion.**

The line graph illustrates how many people visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, over the thirty years from 1990 to 2020.

Overall, visitor numbers rose considerably over the period, although the growth was interrupted by a sharp decline in the mid-2010s. The figure at the end of the period was the highest recorded.

For the first five years the number of visitors remained constant at 200,000. After 1995, however, the figure grew rapidly, reaching 480,000 in 2005, more than double the starting level.

This was followed by a decade of decline. Numbers dipped slightly to 470,000 in 2010 and then fell sharply to 350,000 over the next five years. In the final period the trend reversed, and visitors climbed to a peak of 520,000 in 2020, the highest figure recorded.

In summary, despite the setback after 2010, the park attracted far more visitors at the end of the period than at the beginning.

This line graph is extremely simple — made to explain the basic concept. Real IELTS doesn't give such easy graphs; two or three lines, or a combination of a line graph with another graph, will come. Let's look at those now.

title: Graph with two lines — writing with comparison
blocks: The graph shows the percentage of households owning a car and a bicycle in one European city between 2000 and 2020.
Households owning a car / a bicycle, 2000–2020 (%)

Not only here — after receiving any Task 1, the first job is to understand the topic well. "Percentage of households owning a car and a bicycle" — means the graph shows what percentage of families have a car and what percentage have a bicycle, from 2000 to 2020. Two things to keep in mind: the data is about two different things (car and bicycle), and the data is from the past, so past tense.
Step 2 · Understanding the axes and details

The horizontal axis has years at 5-year intervals (2000, 2005 … 2020). The vertical axis has percentages, from 0 to 100. The two lines go in opposite directions — one is falling, one is rising — and in 2015 they cross each other (crossover). This crossing is the most important feature of the graph.
Car: rose slightly until 2005 (70 → 72), then fell for 15 years (72 → 48).
Bicycle: rose throughout the period (25 → 68), faster after 2005.
2020: bicycle 20 points above car — the exact reverse of the picture in 2000.
The graph has a lot of information and it's not possible to discuss it all (only 20 minutes in hand, and the word limit must be kept in mind too). So these four points are our report.
In the earlier structure: The ___ graph compares/describes + information + measurement + duration + main feature.

The line graph compares the proportion of households owning a car with the proportion owning a bicycle in a European city over two decades from 2000. Car ownership declined while bicycle ownership rose, and the two figures crossed in 2015.
Overall, cars became steadily less common and bicycles steadily more common, so that by the end of the period the bicycle had overtaken the car as the more widely owned of the two.
Many people write the two lines separately in two separate paragraphs, because this seems the easiest. But graph analysis means compare and contrast. Two ways to arrange the body:
By line: para 1 = car, para 2 = bicycle — each compared with the other.
By time: para 1 = 2000–2010, para 2 = 2010–2020 — both lines in each.
If the lines cross or change direction at the same time, "by time" is better, because then the crossover can be described directly. That's what we'll do here.
Start with the car trend, structure: information + verb + adverb + amount + time. Then the bicycle with a contrasting connective:

In 2000, cars were far more common than bicycles: 70% of households had a car, compared with only a quarter that had a bicycle. Car ownership edged up to 72% in 2005 before beginning to decline, falling to 65% by 2010. Meanwhile, bicycle ownership grew steadily, reaching 42% in the same year.

The following decade saw the gap close and then reverse. In 2015 both figures stood at exactly 55%. By 2020, however, car ownership had dropped to under half of households (48%), whereas the bicycle figure had climbed to 68%, twenty percentage points higher.
Language of comparison — what was used in this answer, and more
far more common than · compared with · only a quarter · meanwhile · in the same year · the gap closed · both stood at · whereas · twenty percentage points higher
twice as high as · the reverse was true for · the two lines converged / diverged · X overtook Y · the difference narrowed / widened · X lagged behind Y · X caught up with Y · at the same level as
⚠ **Percentage point:** from 25% to 40%, the increase is "15 percentage points", not "15 percent". (A 15 percent increase means 25 → 28.75.)

The line graph compares the proportion of households owning a car with the proportion owning a bicycle in a European city over two decades from 2000.

Overall, cars became steadily less common and bicycles steadily more common, so that by the end of the period the bicycle had overtaken the car as the more widely owned of the two.

In 2000, cars were far more common than bicycles: 70% of households had a car, compared with only a quarter that had a bicycle. Car ownership edged up to 72% in 2005 before beginning to decline, falling to 65% by 2010. Meanwhile, bicycle ownership grew steadily, reaching 42% in the same year.

The following decade saw the gap close and then reverse. In 2015 both figures stood at exactly 55%. By 2020, however, car ownership had dropped to under half of households (48%), whereas the bicycle figure had climbed to 68%, twenty percentage points higher.

In summary, the positions of the two vehicles were completely reversed over the twenty years.

title: Graph with many lines and future projections
blocks: To make the line graph completely clear, let's look at one more, slightly more complex graph.
The graph shows electricity generated from four sources in one country from 2000 to 2020, with projections to 2030 (terawatt-hours).

"Electricity generated from four sources … with projections" — the graph shows how much electricity was generated from four sources (coal, gas, wind, solar): actual data from 2000 to 2020, and an estimate for 2030. Compared with the earlier graphs this one is complex — but the method is the same.
Step 2 · Understanding the axes and details

Horizontal axis: 10-year intervals, 2000–2030. In the middle, at 2020, there is a dotted line — to its left is the past, to its right the future (the dotted lines are projections). Vertical axis: TWh, 0–120.
Some data is from the past, some from the future — be careful with tense. Past tense for the past. For the future, not will — specific vocabulary:

It is predicted / forecast / estimated / expected / projected / anticipated that X will …
X is expected / projected / forecast / predicted to + verb
The forecast / projection is for X to …
X is likely to …
Four lines — describing them all would go past 200 words. So select carefully, since there are so many trends involved:
Coal: largest at the start (120), then halved (60), projected to be almost zero (15) — the biggest fall.
Gas: rose and overtook coal (100), projected to fall slightly (80).
Wind: from almost zero to 45; projected to double and become the largest (90).
Solar: from zero to 25; projected to almost triple (70).
The main point: a shift from coal to renewables.
The line graph shows how much electricity was produced from coal, gas, wind and solar power in one country between 2000 and 2020, together with forecasts for 2030.

Overall, the country is moving away from coal towards renewable energy. Coal was the leading source at the start but is expected to be the smallest by 2030, while wind is projected to become the largest and gas peaks before declining.
Decide carefully in advance how you will divide the body paragraphs. Two options:
(i) Data for all fuels up to 2020 in para 1, projections in para 2.
(ii) Coal and gas (the large sources) in one para, wind and solar (renewables) in another.
Here we'll take (i), because splitting past/future keeps the tense clear too and makes compare/contrast easier.

In 2000 coal dominated, generating 120 TWh, twice the output of gas, while wind and solar produced almost nothing. Over the next twenty years coal fell by half to 60 TWh, and gas rose steadily to overtake it, reaching 100 TWh in 2020. Wind grew from 2 to 45 TWh in the same period, and solar, which had been zero, reached 25 TWh.

These trends are expected to continue and even accelerate. By 2030 coal is projected to fall to just 15 TWh, and gas is forecast to decline slightly to 80. In contrast, wind is predicted to double to 90 TWh, making it the largest source, and solar is expected to almost triple to 70 TWh.
Notice: para 1 has not a single projection word, while para 2 has one in every sentence (expected, projected, forecast, predicted) — and no word has been repeated.
Introduction paraphrased, one sentence, present tense.
Overview as the second paragraph, without numbers; the big trend + (with several lines) who is at the top/bottom at the end.
Select 4–6 key points (start, end, peak, trough, crossover, biggest change) — not every point.
Every trend sentence has direction + degree + number + time.
No verb, adverb or connective three times.
Preposition check: by / to / at / from…to.
Past data → past tense; projection → expected/projected language.
